turns.en: Vic, thanks so much for joining me. Thanks for having me. I'd love you to take me all the way back to where your initial interest in real estate came from. I was born and raised in Minnesota. My parents were immigrants from India, my dad came to his masters at the University of Minnesota and
turns.zh: Vik，非常感谢你来做客。谢谢你的邀请。我很想请你把时间一路拨回到最初——你对房地产的兴趣是从哪儿来的。我生在 Minnesota、长在 Minnesota，我父母是从 India 来的移民，我爸爸是来 University of Minnesota 读硕士的，

As a kid, I grew up in the real estate business. I'd go to construction sites and see how things were built or we'd go collect rent. I learned
turns.zh: 他本职是工程师，业余会买地、盖房子，主要是独栋住宅（single family home）、联排别墅（townhouse）这一类。作为小孩，我就是在房地产生意里长大的。我会跟着去工地，看房子是怎么盖起来的，或者一起去收租。我很早就

turns.en: real estate at a very early age on the front lines of how things were actually done from building, managing, leasing, so forth. And I became interested when I was in high school. Then when I was 18 years old with my dad, we built our first multi-family project, which was a 48-unit apartment building.
turns.zh: 在一线学会了房地产到底是怎么回事——建造、管理、招租等等。上高中的时候我就产生了兴趣。后来我 18 岁那年，跟我爸一起做了我们第一个多户住宅（multi-family）项目，是一栋 48 户的公寓楼。

turns.en: At that point, I had read a lot of books, I had experienced a lot of things with my dad. I had no history building anything of significance. It was the best experience, but also on the toughest projects because almost anything that could possibly go wrong went wrong from dealing with
turns.zh: 那时候我读了很多书，也跟我爸一起经历了很多事，但我从来没有真正盖过什么有分量的东西。那是最好的经历，同时也是最难的项目，因为几乎所有可能出错的地方都出错了，从跟

turns.en: contractors, construction budgets, it gave me a tremendous experience around how do you actually build things on the front lines, on a hands-on basis. After that, I continued as a developer while I was in college. We built a 124-unit apartment building. I bought and sold different pieces of land
turns.zh: 承包商打交道，到建造预算，这些让我在一线、在亲手实操的层面积累了大量「东西到底是怎么盖起来的」的经验。之后我上大学期间继续做开发，我们盖了一栋 124 户的公寓楼，我也买卖过不同的地块，

turns.en: as well as develop other commercial property all around the Twin Cities area. I always had this vision of building something or renovating something in downtown Minneapolis. We'd identified a historic building that was owned by a family. It was mismanaged and undermanaged. We bought
turns.zh: 也在 Twin Cities 地区各处开发过其他商业地产。我一直有个心愿，想在 Minneapolis 市中心盖点东西或者改造点东西。我们看中了一栋由一个家族持有的历史建筑，它管理得很差、投入也不足。我们在

turns.en: that in 2007 at the worst time possible. Before the financial crisis, and we worked with a lender that we'd done all of our project with. They had a good reputation in Minnesota, and we used historic cash credits to renovate the property. Well, Thesis was building which was really well
turns.zh: 2007 年把它买了下来，那是最糟糕的时点——就在金融危机之前。我们合作的 lender 是一直给我们所有项目融资的那家，他们在 Minnesota 口碑很好，我们还用了历史建筑税收抵免（historic tax credits）来改造这栋物业。这是一栋位置非常好、

turns.en: located, but it was mismanaged as well as not been upgraded for almost 100 years. We'd bring a lot of the systems to market, and that would greatly enhance the value of it. We were one year into the renovation. One day, we wake up, and our lender has been closed in 2008 by the FDIC.
turns.zh: 但管理不善、而且将近 100 年没有升级过的楼。我们打算把很多系统按市场化标准重做，这会大幅提升它的价值。改造进行到第一年的时候，有一天我们醒来，发现我们的 lender 在 2008 年被 FDIC 关闭了。

turns.en: Nothing you could have under rode going into the deal, but it was my first experience into distressed investing and just how unpredictable it can be and how many variables can change and evolve so quickly. That set off a two-year, very litigious process where we were working with the
turns.zh: 这是你进这笔交易时完全没法承做（underwrite）出来的事情，但这也是我第一次接触困境投资，体会到它有多不可预测，有多少变量会那么快地变化和演化。由此引发了一段长达两年、官司缠身的过程，我们要跟

turns.en: FDIC, trying to get them to fund and dealing with a failed bank. We had contractors that had done work, and we had to figure out how do you pay them. At this point in the middle of 2008, there was no chance to bring in a new lender. That took me almost two years to be able to work out.
turns.zh: FDIC 打交道，设法让他们放款，还要应对一家倒闭的银行。我们有承包商已经干了活，就得想办法怎么付钱给他们。而在 2008 年年中那个时点，根本不可能引入新的 lender。这件事我花了将近两年才理清楚。

turns.en: I was 24 years old, rolling up your sleeves and dealing with lawsuits and the FDIC, and I thought about what I wanted to do long-term. Do I start back over again as a entrepreneur and start building real estate in the Twin Cities area, and I decided I was going to move to New York,
turns.zh: 那时我 24 岁，卷起袖子处理诉讼、跟 FDIC 周旋，同时也在想自己长期要做什么：是重新以创业者的身份从头再来、继续在 Twin Cities 地区盖房子，还是……最后我决定搬去 New York，

I didn't want to get my MBA, so I decided to go to a one-year master's in real estate program at Columbia. Knowing that didn't have any relationships, I decided I was going to run for
turns.zh: 在那里我一个人都不认识。有意思的是，年轻的时候你会觉得两年像一辈子那么长。我不想读 MBA，所以决定去 Columbia 读一个一年制的房地产硕士项目。知道自己没有任何人脉，我就决定去竞选

turns.zh: 班长（class president）。我讲了自己创业的经历，讲了我当班长能做什么，最后真的当选了。我觉得这是认识人、建立人脉网络的绝佳方式。有一天我坐在教室里，一个叫 Blake Hutcheson 的人——他现在是

turns.en: CEO of Omers, was talking about the value of relationships. He was saying that a lot of the things that you think about going into grad school is about the things that you learn, but so much of it is about the connections in those last a lifetime. He was talking about his best friend who he
turns.zh: OMERS 的 CEO——在讲人际关系的价值。他说，很多人进研究生院时想的是能学到什么，但其实很大一部分价值在于人脉，而这些关系会伴随你一生。他讲到他最好的朋友，是

turns.en: had met while was in the same program at Columbia, a guy named Mark Mugoldrek, who was the co-founder of the special sits group at Goldman, this legendary investor. turns.zh: 他在 Columbia 同一个项目读书时认识的，叫 Mark McGoldrick，是 Goldman 特殊情况（special situations）团队的联合创始人，一位传奇投资人。他在亚洲金融危机期间声名大噪，做各种困境投资和机会型投资（opportunistic investing）。当我

turns.en: I was hearing this as a boy, this guy sounds like he can walk on a water. It was just unbelievable his story and the deals that he was doing. I went to Blake after a class as it could you introduce him to Mark and so he gives me his business car. He sure emailed me. He emailed a couple of times.
turns.zh: 作为一个年轻人听到这些时，觉得这个人简直能在水上行走。他的故事、他做的那些交易，太不可思议了。下课后我跑去找 Blake，问他能不能把我介绍给 Mark，他就给了我他的名片，说当然可以，他会发邮件；他发了几封，

They said, we know who he is, but we've had no connection with him from almost 20 years. Eventually, Blake had introduced me to Mark. At this
turns.zh: 但没有回音。我就想，不行，我得想办法见到他。我去找 Columbia 的校方，问他们跟 Mark 有没有联系。他们说，我们知道他是谁，但差不多 20 年没有来往了。最后 Blake 还是把我介绍给了 Mark。那时

turns.en: point, he had left Goldman. He had started a firm called Malkella, which was effectively a spin-off Goldman special sits. He had raised almost $3 billion dollars the week after Lehman failed. He followed that up by raising another almost $4 billion dollars a few years later.
turns.zh: 他已经离开了 Goldman，创办了一家叫 Mount Kellet 的公司，实际上就是 Goldman 特殊情况团队的分拆（spin-off）。在 Lehman 倒闭后的那一周，他募到了将近 30 亿美元；几年之后他又募了将近 40 亿美元。

turns.en: I met Mark. He was supposed to be a 30-minute coffee and started off as an awkward introduction because he was not the most warm and welcoming person. I told him about my life as an entrepreneur and how I started at a very young age. That business didn't go as planned and blew up during
turns.zh: 我见到了 Mark，本来只是一场 30 分钟的咖啡会面，一开始还挺尴尬的，因为他并不是那种特别热情好客的人。我跟他讲了我作为创业者的经历，讲我怎么很小就开始干，那门生意没有按计划走，在

turns.en: the financial crisis. We talked a lot about our philosophy of life and investing. Keep in mind, at that point, I had no experience in any sort of institutional business. I knew how to use Excel, but very high level and end up being a four-hour meeting. At the end of it, he said, why don't you come
turns.zh: 金融危机中爆掉了。我们聊了很多关于人生和投资的哲学。要知道，那时候我完全没有任何机构化业务的经验，Excel 会用，但只是很浅的水平。结果那场会面聊了四个小时。结束时他说，你不如来

turns.en: work for me as a part-time intern? What aspects of that meeting resonated that bubbled up from a half-hour with a guy who's really busy to afford our conversation? Sometimes when you're an outsider into something you look at it, how it could be versus how it is. A lot of times when people
turns.zh: 给我做兼职实习生。／那场会面里到底是什么打动了他，让一个非常忙的人从原本半小时的安排里挤出时间来跟你深聊？／有时候，当你是一个领域的局外人，你看它的方式是「它可以是什么样」，而不是「它现在是什么样」。很多时候，当人

turns.en: are in a system, they accept a lot of things, this is norm, and this is exactly how things are done. I looked at an industry where I said, there's so many things that don't make sense to me. My whole career up into that point had been thinking like a principal. I saw that with my parents
turns.zh: 身处一个体系之内时，他们会接受很多东西：这就是常态，事情就是这么办的。而我看着这个行业，心里想的是，有太多东西在我看来根本说不通。我到那时为止的整段职业生涯都是以 principal（自己出钱的老板）的方式在思考。这一点我是从我父母身上看到的——

turns.en: being immigrants, buying and building real estate. I looked at the alignment that I would see in a lot of these firms did not make any sense to me. The focus on AUM growth did not make any sense to me because I was an outsider into this industry, especially for somebody at that stage of their life.
turns.zh: 他们是移民，买房、盖房。我看到很多机构里的利益一致（alignment）安排，在我看来完全说不通；他们对管理规模（AUM）增长的执念，在我看来也完全说不通。因为我是这个行业的局外人，尤其对处在我那个阶段的人来说更是如此。

turns.en: That was something I probably Mark had never heard before, and it was less about, here's my resume. I went to the best school, I'm an Excel genius versus just more philosophical that then turned into a huge crossroads in my career that changed the entire trajectory of my life. When you stepped in
turns.zh: 这些东西 Mark 大概从来没听别人讲过，而且它不是在讲「看看我的简历，我上的是最好的学校，我是 Excel 天才」，而更多是理念层面的东西。后来这成了我职业生涯里一个巨大的十字路口，改变了我整个人生的轨迹。／当你走进

turns.en: to work with Mark at Mount Kelet, what did you start to see sitting in an institutional seat for the first time that you hadn't been exposed to as an entrepreneur? I was working with some of the best and brightest minds, specifically in Distressed Investing, and that point,
turns.zh: Mount Kellet 跟 Mark 一起工作、第一次坐在机构投资人的位置上时，你看到了哪些当创业者时接触不到的东西？／我当时是在跟一批最优秀、最聪明的人共事，尤其是在困境投资这个领域。那时候

turns.en: Mount Kelet was $8 billion, special sits firm, investing in all asset classes throughout the world, had this incredibly prestigious reputation. I remember the first day I showed up, the HR person was like, who are you? I never saw my resume. Literally, it was like, why don't you just start on
turns.zh: Mount Kellet 是一家 80 亿美元的特殊情况投资公司，在全球所有资产类别里投资，声誉极其显赫。我记得第一天去报到，HR 跟我说：你是谁？我从没见过你的简历。真的是这样，然后就说，那你不如

turns.en: a Monday? That was Mark's philosophy, even from the early days of Goldman, if I believe in somebody, and it's a true meritocracy, then you have the ability to rise to the top. turns.zh: 周一就开始吧。这就是 Mark 的理念，从他在 Goldman 的早期就是如此：如果我认可一个人，而这里又 truly 是精英制（meritocracy），那你就有能力一路升到最上面。我从第一天起就知道，我绝不可能靠技术能力最强而出人头地。

turns.en: You had people that were geniuses in Excel, and memos, and underwriting. I thought to myself, even as an intern, what can I do to create value and to separate myself from everyone else? There was two ways. I have to find some unique deals that either Mount Kelet or other firms don't
turns.zh: 那里有在 Excel、写投资备忘录（memo）、承做（underwriting）上是天才的人。我就问自己，哪怕只是个实习生，我能做什么来创造价值、把自己和其他人区分开？只有两条路：要么找到一些独特的交易，是 Mount Kellet 或者其他机构

turns.en: necessarily have access to, or I have to find capital. What happened from there? Within two years,
turns.zh: 不一定接触得到的；要么去找资金。有三个月我就专注在这上面，找到了几个有意思的机会，最后我们真的投了，也让我从 Columbia 毕业后正式全职加入 Mount Kellet。／后来呢？／两年之内，

turns.en: I was co-head of US Real Estate Investments, which was about 25% of the firm's capital, and it was an incredible experience because I learned from Mark and some of the best distressed investors in the world, and that shaped so much of my thinking around how to invest,
turns.zh: 我就成了美国房地产投资的联席负责人，那块大约占公司资金的 25%。那是难以置信的经历，因为我跟着 Mark 以及世界上一些最好的困境投资人学习，这极大地塑造了我关于如何投资的思考，
